There are 17 possible configurations. To see this, treat "friends" (which includes frenemies) as one relation F and "enemies" (which includes frenemies) as another relation E. Every pair lies in F, in E, or in both.

**Structure of F.** The first rule says F is transitive, so F splits the five people into classes, and everyone within a class is mutually friends. Any pair in different classes is not in F, so it must be enemies only.

**Enemy pairs inside a class.** Suppose A and B are in the same class and are also enemies. Take any C in that class. Then C and A are friends and A and B are enemies, so the third rule makes C and B enemies. Repeating the argument shows every pair in that class is also enemies. So a class either has no internal enemy pairs, or it is entirely frenemies.

**Number of classes.** Suppose there were three classes, with A, B, C one from each. All three cross pairs are enemy-only. Then A–B and B–C are enemies, so the second rule forces A and C to be friends, which contradicts them being in different classes. So there are at most 2 classes.

**Two classes.** Suppose one class X is all frenemies and has size at least 2, and the other class Y is nonempty. Take A, B in X and C in Y. Then A and B are enemies, and B and C are enemies, so the second rule forces A and C to be friends. That contradicts them being in different classes. So with two classes, both are purely friends internally and all cross pairs are enemies. The second rule then holds because any two people who are both enemies of a third lie in the same class. The number of ways to split 5 people into two nonempty unordered groups is 2⁴ − 1 = 15.

**One class.** The class is either all friends or all frenemies, giving 2 configurations.

The total is 15 + 2 = 17.

ANSWER: 17
